desc:
Encoding. A singly linked list is passed to your function as an array holding the node values from head to tail; an empty array is an empty list. You may build real nodes from it first, or work on the array directly. The result is also returned as an array of values from head to tail.

You are given a list of operations, each written as [l, r, k]. An operation takes the sublist made of the nodes at 0-based positions l through r (inclusive) and rotates only that sublist to the right by k places: one step moves the last node of the sublist to the front of the sublist. Nodes outside the range do not move.

Apply the operations in the given order and return the final values. For example nums = [1,2,3,4,5] with ops = [[1,3,1],[0,4,2]] first gives [1,4,2,3,5] (the sublist 2,3,4 becomes 4,2,3) and then [3,5,1,4,2].
constraints: 0 ≤ l ≤ r < nums.length for every operation
hints: A single operation is the 'rotate list' problem on a sublist, and k can be huge, so reduce it first.
For a sublist of length m = r - l + 1 only k mod m matters. If it is 0, skip the operation.

Cut the sublist out (keep the node before l and the node after r), rotate it by relinking its tail to its head and breaking the ring m - k mod m steps in, and splice it back between the two kept neighbours.
editorial: Each operation is independent of the others in structure, so process them one after another. For an operation reduce k modulo the sublist length m; when the result is 0 nothing changes.

Otherwise the last s = k mod m nodes of the sublist become its first s nodes. With real pointers: find the node before position l and the node at position r, find the node at offset m - s - 1 inside the sublist (the new tail of the sublist), and re-hook three links: the old sublist tail to the old sublist head, the new sublist tail to the node after r, and the node before l to the new sublist head. One operation costs O(r) to walk to the segment, so the total is O(q · n) time with O(1) extra space; with 2,000 operations on 3,000 nodes this is fast.
